title: Stop hook appends a session entry as five separate writes, so concurrent sessions interleave in the daily memory file
reason: One journal entry written as five `echo`s can interleave with a concurrent session's entry, splitting a summary from its anchor. capture.append_to_journal builds the whole block in memory and emits it with a single `handle.write(f"{block}{summary}\n\n")` into an O_APPEND handle (capture.py:334-344) — exactly the fix upstream proposes; the golden tests at tests/test_capture.py:494-560 pin that byte layout. (A summary larger than the 8 KB stdio buffer would still be split into two writes, as upstream's printf fix would too; bullets never come close.)

title: Daily memory filename collides across machines sharing a synced .memsearch/memory/ folder
reason: Two machines sharing one synced memory dir append to the same YYYY-MM-DD.md, and a file-level sync client resolves that as a conflicted copy or last-writer-wins. Fork counterpart: capture.append_to_journal (capture.py:330) hardcodes `f"{stamp:%Y-%m-%d}.md"`, so the fork has the same failure mode; the fix is a small opt-in knob, not a subsystem, so it is the user's call.
action:
PROPOSAL — opt-in per-writer suffix on the daily journal filename.
What: add `memory.filename_suffix` (default "", accepted values "" or "hostname") to config.py's dataclasses, and in capture.append_to_journal compose the name as `f"{stamp:%Y-%m-%d}{suffix}.md"` where a `hostname` suffix expands to `-{socket.gethostname().split('.')[0]}` (sanitised to [A-Za-z0-9_-]). Also widen hooks._DAILY_JOURNAL (hooks.py:34) from `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}\.md$` to `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}(-[A-Za-z0-9_-]+)?\.md$`, or the SessionStart Recent Memory injection silently stops seeing the suffixed journals (the indexer and search do not care: scanner takes every *.md).
Why: two machines appending to one synced .memsearch/memory (iCloud/Dropbox/Syncthing on the project dir, or one MEMSEARCH_DIR on a synced path — a setup the README documents under 'One memory for many projects') is a last-writer-wins data loss with no error. The fork's single-write append protects one machine's kernel, not two file-sync clients.
Cost: ~10 lines in capture.py + 1 regex + 2 config fields, no new dependency; two tests (suffixed filename; recent_memory still picks the file up).
If not done: multi-machine users silently lose turn summaries; the workaround is to give each machine its own MEMSEARCH_DIR, which also splits search.
Note the fork's README scopes it to 'a single machine', so declining this on scope is equally defensible.

title: Memory summary unavailable: dsh headless summarization timed out; transcript content was omitted. Use the transcript anchor for progressive disclosure.

title: macOS Seatbelt sandbox: both orphan-reaping paths fail silently, watch processes accumulate without bound
reason: Under a macOS Seatbelt sandbox both of stop_watch's orphan-reaping arms (pgrep and kill -0) fail silently, so `memsearch watch` processes accumulate. title: Claude Code plugin: watch pidfile lives inside the watched dir, so removing a git worktree orphans its watcher permanently (34 leaked trees / 6.7 GB observed)

The analogous state is <project>/.memsearch/index.lock, an flock held only for the duration of one index run (cli.py:69-82) and released by the kernel when the process exits, so deleting the tree can leak nothing.

title: Claude Code SessionStart hook still hits `timeout: 10` after #645 — `--version` is a second full CLI boot and the PyPI check blocks (~3.4s of ~4.9s is avoidable)
reason: SessionStart hits the 10 s timeout because ~3.4 s of the blocking path is avoidable: a second full CLI boot for `memsearch --version` and a synchronous PyPI request for an update banner (plus a 1.5 s pymilvus/pandas import). Measured: the bash prologue of session-start.sh (common.sh + hook_guard + have_uv + venv_ready) is ~9 ms per run; after that it execs one `uv run --frozen --no-sync` whose work is one `git rev-parse` (2 s cap), one read-only sqlite query and two journal reads.

title: tests: subprocess.run(["bash", ...]) fails with WinError 2 outside Git Bash on Windows
reason: Tests calling subprocess.run(["bash", ...]) fail outside Git Bash on Windows; the fix is to resolve bash via shutil.which. title: Claude and Codex hooks resolve different project roots outside a git repo (fork memory store)
reason: Outside a git repo the Claude and Codex bash hooks resolved the project root differently (CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR vs the payload cwd), silently splitting one project into two stores. The fork has one implementation for both hosts — hooks.resolve_project_dir (hooks.py:88-108), same precedence (CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR > payload cwd > process cwd, then the git root) for --platform claude and --platform codex, pinned by tests/test_hooks.py:197-221 — and upstream's preferred option 1 exists as MEMSEARCH_DIR, honored by both hooks (hooks.memsearch_dir, hooks.py:111-113) and by both memory-recall skills, and documented in README 'One memory for many projects'.

title: Claude Code plugin: Stop-hook summarizer re-triggers plugin hooks, scattering phantom session headers (and a stray watcher + junk collection) into ~/.memsearch
reason: The Stop hook's `claude -p` summarizer is a full session that re-fires the plugin's own hooks, scattering empty '## Session' headings (in the home dir when the child resolves no repo) plus a stray watcher and a junk collection. The fork kills all three: the summarizer child is spawned with MEMSEARCH_DISABLE=1 and CLAUDECODE="" (capture.py:249) and every launcher exits on hook_guard (hooks/common.sh:69-75, mirrored by hooks._disabled at hooks.py:273), SessionStart never writes to the journal (hooks.py:340-343 only mkdirs — the heading is written lazily by capture.append_to_journal:333-334 with a real summary), the child runs with cwd=project_dir (hooks.py:365), and there is no watcher and no collection to create.

title: Windows: kill_orphaned_index can't reap native index processes (Git Bash) -> unbounded accumulation / OOM
reason: kill_orphaned_index cannot reap native Windows index processes under Git Bash, so per-turn `memsearch index` processes accumulate until OOM. The fork has no reaper because it needs none: every background index runs with --skip-if-locked and a non-blocking flock on <project>/.memsearch/index.lock (cli.py:69-82, hooks.py:120-121), so a second indexer exits immediately instead of piling up. Windows is out of scope anyway (cli.py:10 imports fcntl).

title: Claude Code: SessionStart writes an empty `## Session HH:MM` heading every session, polluting Recent Memory injection and the search index
reason: SessionStart appends '## Session HH:MM' unconditionally while the body is only written on a captured turn, so empty headings accumulate and dominate both the Recent Memory injection and the index. In the fork SessionStart writes nothing to the journal at all (hooks.session_start only does memory.mkdir, hooks.py:340-343); the heading is created lazily by the entry that carries a summary (capture.py:333-334, golden test tests/test_capture.py:494-533). Belt and braces: hooks._preview_sections only emits a section that has at least one bullet (hooks.py:198-219, tests/test_hooks.py:355).

title: MilvusStore.upsert() reports success but writes are not durable on remote Milvus 2.5+ (missing flush)
reason: MilvusStore.upsert() returns a fabricated success count while remote Milvus 2.5+ never flushed the rows, so 'Indexed 219 chunks' coexists with row_count 0. There is no Milvus here. The equivalent claim in the fork cannot drift from reality: Store.upsert returns the rows it actually executed inside a committed BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction (store.py:312-337, _write commits at store.py:186-193) and index_paths sums those returns (store.py:491-499).

title: Stop hook writes Anthropic API rate-limit error string as memory summary content
reason: When `claude -p` answers a rate limit with a human sentence on stdout and exits 0, the hook writes that sentence into the journal as the turn's summary, and it is then embedded and returned by recall. The fork is exposed the same way: capture.summarize only rejects a non-zero exit and empty output (capture.py:278-281) and hooks._summarize_and_append writes whatever comes back (hooks.py:360-379), so a single non-bullet line still lands in <project>/.memsearch/memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md. Low severity (it needs a rate limit or a refusal that exits 0) but the guard is four lines and the degraded path already exists.
action: capture.summarize now rejects summarizer output that contains no bullet line (`- `, `* ` or `• `) with the reason 'summarizer returned no bullet points'; hooks then write the standard 'Memory summary unavailable' line (Codex: mechanical fallback first). title: Stop hook's `claude -p` summarize call fires SessionStart, polluting daily logs and leaking to nested directories

title: feat: derive project scope from git-common-dir so worktrees share one memory
reason: Linked worktrees each derive their own project dir from `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`, so memory fragments per worktree and dies with `git worktree remove`; upstream closed this as not planned, keeping defaults directory-scoped. The fork has the same derivation (hooks.resolve_project_dir, hooks.py:97-107) and no per-project config layer to pin, so the question stands on its own here and it is a feature decision, not a bug.
action:
PROPOSAL — make linked worktrees of one repo share the primary checkout's memory.
What: in hooks.resolve_project_dir (hooks.py:97-107), after `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`, run `git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-dir --git-common-dir` and, only when the two differ (which is exactly the linked-worktree case), use `dirname(common_dir)` as the project dir. Comparing the two values is what keeps submodules safe: there git-dir == git-common-dir == <super>/.git/modules/<name>, so nothing changes; a naive dirname(git-common-dir) would corrupt them.
Why: one worktree per agent is this repo's own workflow. Today each worktree gets its own <worktree>/.memsearch/memory and its own index.db, so what an agent learned on one branch is invisible on the next and `git worktree remove` deletes that corpus. The fork's only sharing knob, MEMSEARCH_DIR, is all-or-nothing: it merges every project into one store.
Cost: ~8 lines in one function, no new dependency, no index rebuild for primary checkouts (the path they hash is unchanged); two tests (linked worktree resolves to the primary root; a submodule still resolves to the submodule root). The concurrency half of this upstream issue is already covered — capture.append_to_journal writes one entry in one write() (see #727).
If not done: worktree memory stays fragmented, which is the status quo and what upstream chose.
Caveats to decide: journals already written inside existing worktrees stay where they are (they would need a manual move), and a worktree used for an unrelated experiment would start writing into the primary repo's journal. An env opt-in (MEMSEARCH_SHARE_WORKTREES=1) is possible but adds a knob.

title: fix: support flat transcript content
reason: Concept: accept transcript events whose `content` sits at the top level instead of under `message`, for VSCode Copilot's Claude-Code-hook compatibility layer (upstream #221). title: fix: fail open when hook stdin is absent
reason: Concept: a hook invoked without stdin must fail open at once instead of waiting out the `timeout 2 cat` / perl-alarm fallback. title: fix: scope index-process cleanup to the running harness
reason: Concept: two harnesses sharing one MEMSEARCH_DIR reap each other's in-flight index because the pidfile and the pgrep sweeps are harness-blind. The fork never kills anything — hooks.py spawns `index <memory> --skip-if-locked` and cli.py:_index_lock takes a non-blocking flock on <project>/.memsearch/index.lock, so the second harness gives up quietly instead of killing the first, and staleness (hooks.py:_index_state, mtime > last_index_at) makes the next SessionStart pick up whatever the skipped run missed.

title: fix(hooks): keep the watch registry outside the watched tree

title: fix: strict upsert accounting and opt-in end-of-index flush
reason: Concept: index reports success while nothing became durable, plus a cross-process read-after-write gap. Both are Milvus artefacts. Store.upsert (store.py) writes inside a BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction that either commits or raises and returns the number of rows it actually wrote, and once committed in WAL mode a separate process sees the rows immediately — there is no server-reported count to distrust and nothing to flush.

title: feat: merge undersized heading sections during chunking (chunking.min_chunk_size)
reason: Concept applies squarely: heading-dense journals (the fork's `### HH:MM` turn sections) produce one chunk per section no matter how tiny, so a day of short turns costs one embedding each. Upstream adds an opt-in chunking.min_chunk_size that accumulates consecutive undersized sections into one chunk, default 0 = today's behaviour exactly. Draft upstream, and the author flags that a maintainer-side retrieval eval would be worth running before recommending a non-zero default.
action: PROPOSAL — add `chunking.min_chunk_size` (default 0 = no change). What: in chunker.chunk_markdown, accumulate consecutive sections whose text is below min_chunk_size into one Chunk (never crossing max_chunk_size), keeping the first section's heading and the merged line span; oversized sections keep routing through _split_large_section. Why: the fork's journals are the exact shape that motivates it — every turn is a `### HH:MM` section of 2-4 bullets, so each turn is its own embedding and its own row; merging a session's turns into one chunk cuts index size and embedding time several-fold and gives search a section of context instead of two bullets. Cost: ~25 lines in chunker.py, 2 lines in config.py (ChunkingConfig.min_chunk_size + _INT_FIELDS), ~4 lines threading it through store.index_paths/_index_file and cli.index, one README config-table row, ~40 lines of tests (default keeps per-section behaviour; tiny sections merge with the right heading and line span; merge respects max_chunk_size; a pending merge flushes before an oversized section). No new dependency. If not done: nothing breaks — this is a cost/quality tuning knob, not a bug. Caveat: chunk ids hash content + line span, so switching it on re-embeds the affected files once (`index --force`), and retrieval quality is corpus-dependent — recommend shipping it with default 0 and trying, say, 400 by hand first.

title: perf: raise ONNX default batch size to 64
reason: Raises OnnxEmbedding._DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE from 32 to 64 (~11% faster indexing on the default gpahal/bge-m3-onnx-int8 CPU export, measured upstream). The fork ships the same class with the same 32 and the same default provider, so the measurement transfers directly.
action: PROPOSAL — change OnnxEmbedding._DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE from 32 to 64 in src/memsearch/embeddings/onnx.py. What: one constant; `embedding.batch_size` in config.toml keeps overriding it and 0 still means 'provider default'. Why: onnx is the fork's default provider and the first index of a real journal set is the slowest thing the plugin ever does; upstream measured 13.2s -> 11.7s per 128 texts on CPU. Memory risk is bounded here: the tokenizer pads to the longest text in the batch, and the fork's chunks are capped at chunking.max_chunk_size (1500 chars), so a 64-wide batch stays small — upstream refused 128 only because of the 8192-token worst case, which arbitrary `memsearch index <path>` targets could still hit. Cost: 1 line, plus ~10 lines of test asserting the default and that batch_size= still overrides. If not done: indexing stays ~10% slower; no correctness impact.

title: feat: auto-select ONNX execution providers with CPU-safe fallback
reason: OnnxEmbedding builds its InferenceSession with no `providers` argument, so onnxruntime never uses an accelerator even when the installed build has one. Upstream selects from an allowlist (CUDA first, CPU always appended, Azure and CoreML never auto-picked) and retries CPU-only if accelerator session creation fails. The fork has the identical line (onnx.py: `ort.InferenceSession(model_path)`).
action: PROPOSAL — auto-select ONNX execution providers with a CPU fallback in src/memsearch/embeddings/onnx.py. What: a pure `_select_providers(available, requested=None)` helper — keep CUDAExecutionProvider when present, always append CPUExecutionProvider, never auto-pick AzureExecutionProvider (remote) or CoreML (upstream measured it ~60x SLOWER than CPU on this int8 bge-m3 export) — then `ort.InferenceSession(model_path, providers=_select_providers(ort.get_available_providers()))` with a CPU-only retry if that raises. Cost: ~20 lines in onnx.py plus ~30 lines of pure-function tests (no onnxruntime needed); upstream's version is +64/-2 because it also adds a `providers=` constructor argument, which I would drop — get_provider() forwards kwargs by signature and there is no config key for it, so it would be unreachable. Why it may not be worth it: the fork's onnx extra pins the CPU-only onnxruntime wheel, so the change is a no-op unless the user swaps in onnxruntime-gpu by hand; the honest gain is the explicit CPU fallback and never letting a remote provider be picked implicitly. If not done: embedding stays CPU-bound, which is what the README already promises.

title: test: cover transcript formatting edge cases
reason: Concept: user message text in a Claude Code transcript carries harness-injected tag blocks, and upstream strips them (`_strip_hook_tags`) before rendering a turn, dropping the turn when nothing is left. The fork's src/memsearch/transcript.py renders user text verbatim, so those blocks are spent against the head-truncated 12,000-char MAX_RENDER_CHARS budget of `memsearch transcript` — measured over the 12 most recent real transcripts in ~/.claude/projects, 76 of 128 user turns carry such blocks and 54.6% of all user-turn characters sit inside them, so L3 recall can lose the actual conversation to harness noise.
action: transcript.strip_harness_tags removes harness-injected blocks (system-reminder, command-name/message/args, local-command-stdout/caveat, task-notification) from Claude user entries — an explicit allowlist, so user-authored tags survive — in both the L3 render (transcript._parse_claude) and the summarizer input (capture._claude_texts). reason: Earlier, weaker version of pr#231: DEFAULT_MODELS assertions plus an unknown-provider ValueError, with the provider-instantiation tests skipped unless an API key is present. title: test: add nested directory scanning coverage
reason: Deep (5-level) and wide (10-sibling) directory scanning. scan_paths() walks with os.walk and its recursion is pinned by tests/test_scanner.py::test_scan_finds_markdown_files_recursively; extra depth and breadth are scale, not behaviour.

title: ci: add pre-commit hooks for ruff lint and format
reason: Pre-commit hooks running ruff lint and format. The fork already carries .pre-commit-config.yaml with the same two hooks (commit ef62750, 'ci: add pre-commit hooks for ruff lint and format'), pinned to a current ruff-pre-commit rev and using the modern `ruff-check` id instead of the deprecated `ruff`; .github/workflows/test.yml runs `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` directly, so pre-commit is a local convenience and is deliberately not a dev dependency. The PR's unrelated README tip and pytest-cov line have no counterpart here.

title: test(chunker): add coverage for compute_chunk_id behavior
reason: Two halves. The scanner half (empty path list, missing path, custom extensions, hidden files, mtime/size, _maybe_add dedup) is fully covered by tests/test_scanner.py. The chunker half asserts compute_chunk_id is model-sensitive, which is deliberately false here: the fork dropped the model component so a model change rebuilds the index instead of doubling every row — tests/test_chunk_id_format.py::test_chunk_id_takes_no_model_argument and ::test_chunk_id_varies_with_every_component pin that.

title: Stop hook writes Anthropic API rate-limit error string as memory summary content
reason: When `claude -p` answers a rate limit with a human sentence on stdout and exits 0, the hook writes that sentence into the journal as the turn's summary, and it is then embedded and returned by recall. The fork is exposed the same way: capture.summarize only rejects a non-zero exit and empty output (capture.py:278-281) and hooks._summarize_and_append writes whatever comes back (hooks.py:360-379), so a single non-bullet line still lands in <project>/.memsearch/memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md. Low severity (it needs a rate limit or a refusal that exits 0) but the guard is four lines and the degraded path already exists.
action: capture.summarize now rejects summarizer output that contains no bullet line (`- `, `* ` or `• `) with the reason 'summarizer returned no bullet points'; hooks then write the standard 'Memory summary unavailable' line (Codex: mechanical fallback first). Files: src/memsearch/capture.py; tests: tests/test_capture.py (prose with exit 0, bullet markers), tests/test_hooks.py (journal never contains the rate-limit notice).

title: test: cover transcript formatting edge cases
reason: Concept: user message text in a Claude Code transcript carries harness-injected tag blocks, and upstream strips them (`_strip_hook_tags`) before rendering a turn, dropping the turn when nothing is left. The fork's src/memsearch/transcript.py renders user text verbatim, so those blocks are spent against the head-truncated 12,000-char MAX_RENDER_CHARS budget of `memsearch transcript` — measured over the 12 most recent real transcripts in ~/.claude/projects, 76 of 128 user turns carry such blocks and 54.6% of all user-turn characters sit inside them, so L3 recall can lose the actual conversation to harness noise.
action: transcript.strip_harness_tags removes harness-injected blocks (system-reminder, command-name/message/args, local-command-stdout/caveat, task-notification) from Claude user entries — an explicit allowlist, so user-authored tags survive — in both the L3 render (transcript._parse_claude) and the summarizer input (capture._claude_texts). Files: src/memsearch/transcript.py, src/memsearch/capture.py; tests: tests/test_transcript.py (5 cases), tests/test_capture.py.

title: perf: raise ONNX default batch size to 64
reason: Raises OnnxEmbedding._DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE from 32 to 64 (~11% faster indexing on the default gpahal/bge-m3-onnx-int8 CPU export, measured upstream). The fork ships the same class with the same 32 and the same default provider, so the measurement transfers directly.
action: OnnxEmbedding._DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE raised from 32 to 64 (embedding.batch_size still overrides); install hint now points at 'uv sync --extra onnx'. Files: src/memsearch/embeddings/onnx.py; test: tests/test_embeddings_onnx_inputs.py.

title: feat: auto-select ONNX execution providers with CPU-safe fallback
reason: OnnxEmbedding builds its InferenceSession with no `providers` argument, so onnxruntime never uses an accelerator even when the installed build has one. Upstream selects from an allowlist (CUDA first, CPU always appended, Azure and CoreML never auto-picked) and retries CPU-only if accelerator session creation fails. The fork has the identical line (onnx.py: `ort.InferenceSession(model_path)`).
action: OnnxEmbedding builds its session with an explicit provider list (_select_providers: CUDA when available, always ending with CPU; Azure/CoreML never auto-selected) and retries on CPU if the accelerator fails to load. Files: src/memsearch/embeddings/onnx.py; test: tests/test_embeddings_onnx_inputs.py.

title: feat: derive project scope from git-common-dir so worktrees share one memory
reason: Linked worktrees each derive their own project dir from `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`, so memory fragments per worktree and dies with `git worktree remove`; upstream closed this as not planned, keeping defaults directory-scoped. The fork has the same derivation (hooks.resolve_project_dir, hooks.py:97-107) and no per-project config layer to pin, so the question stands on its own here and it is a feature decision, not a bug.
action: hooks.resolve_project_dir maps a linked git worktree to its primary checkout (git-dir != git-common-dir), so all worktrees of a repository share one .memsearch; submodules keep their own. Files: src/memsearch/hooks.py; tests: tests/test_hooks.py (worktree, submodule).

title: Daily memory filename collides across machines sharing a synced .memsearch/memory/ folder
reason: Two machines sharing one synced memory dir append to the same YYYY-MM-DD.md, and a file-level sync client resolves that as a conflicted copy or last-writer-wins. Fork counterpart: capture.append_to_journal (capture.py:330) hardcodes `f"{stamp:%Y-%m-%d}.md"`, so the fork has the same failure mode; the fix is a small opt-in knob, not a subsystem, so it is the user's call.
action: New memory.filename_suffix config (\\ or \hostname\): journals become YYYY-MM-DD-<short host>.md so machines sharing a synced memory folder never overwrite each other; the recent-memory pattern accepts the suffix. Files: src/memsearch/{config,capture,hooks}.py, README.md; tests: tests/test_{config,capture,hooks}.py.
